title: IF GOD IS FOR YOU, WHY DOES IT FEEL LIKE EVERYTHING IS AGAINST YOU?
paragraphs: IF GOD IS FOR YOU, WHY DOES IT FEEL LIKE EVERYTHING IS AGAINST YOU?
Paul Never Promised You Would Have No Enemies. He Revealed Something Far More Powerful: Even Your Worst Enemy Cannot Overturn What Jesus Christ Has Already Secured.
There is a Bible verse that sounds beautiful until you are standing in the middle of a life that seems determined to contradict it.
“If God be for us, who can be against us?” — Romans 8:31 (KJV)
You have probably heard it preached with confidence. Maybe you have seen it printed on a shirt, written across a photograph of a sunrise, or spoken over someone preparing for a difficult season.
It sounds like victory.
It sounds like protection.
It almost sounds like a promise that nothing terrible will happen to people who belong to God.
But what happens when you love Jesus and people still betray you?
What happens when you pray, and the diagnosis does not change?
When you choose forgiveness, and the person who wounded you never apologizes?
When you try to live faithfully, yet the doors keep closing, the bills keep coming, and the people you trusted become the very people speaking against you?
What happens when you are doing your best to follow Christ, but your life looks less like a victory celebration and more like a battlefield?
There is a kind of pain that becomes even heavier when you believe you are not supposed to be experiencing it.
You start asking questions you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Lord, if You are really for me, why does it feel like so much is against me?”
And somewhere in the silence, another question begins to form.
“Did I misunderstand Your promise? Or have You stopped loving me?”
If you have ever wrestled with those questions, Romans 8 was written for a world much closer to yours than you might imagine.
Because when the apostle Paul wrote those unforgettable words, he was not sitting comfortably in a world without opposition.
He knew what it meant to be hated.
He knew what it meant to suffer for the name of Jesus.
He knew hunger, danger, persecution, imprisonment, and the terrible loneliness of being abandoned.
And yet, with full knowledge of what following Christ could cost, he wrote:
“If God be for us, who can be against us?”
Not because he had no enemies.
But because he knew something his enemies could never change.
And if you understand what Paul actually meant, you may never read that verse the same way again.
The answer begins with a word that is easy to overlook.
In the Greek text of Romans 8:31, Paul writes:
Ei ho Theos hyper hēmōn, tis kath’ hēmōn?
“If God is for us, who is against us?”
The word ὑπέρ (hyper) carries the sense of being for, on behalf of, or in support of someone.
And the expression καθ’ ἡμῶν (kath’ hēmōn) means against us.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say nobody will oppose us.
He does not say nobody will accuse us.
He does not say nobody will hurt us.
He asks a question whose answer must be understood in light of everything he has just said about God's saving purpose.
If God Himself has acted decisively on our behalf through Jesus Christ, who can successfully overturn His saving verdict?
That is the force of Paul's argument.
Not the absence of opposition.
The inability of opposition to defeat God's purpose for those who belong to Christ.
And that difference matters more than most of us realize.
Because some of us have spent years believing that the presence of enemies must mean the absence of God.
We thought that if we were obedient enough, prayerful enough, faithful enough, then surely the road would become easier.
We thought being blessed meant being untouched.
We thought being favored meant being universally accepted.
We thought having God on our side meant never being brought to our knees.
But the Bible never teaches that God's children are immune to suffering.
In fact, Jesus said something remarkably different.
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33 (KJV)
Jesus did not hide the tribulation.
He announced it.
And then He pointed to His victory.
He did not say, “You will never face trouble.”
He said, in effect, “Trouble will come, but it will not have the final word.”
Think about that.
The Savior who promised victory was Himself rejected, mocked, falsely accused, betrayed, beaten, and crucified.
If opposition were proof that God had abandoned someone, what would we do with Calvary?
What would we do with the sinless Son of God hanging between criminals while religious leaders mocked Him and soldiers divided His garments?
What would we do with the disciples who watched the One they loved suffer a death that looked, to human eyes, like absolute defeat?
And yet the cross was not evidence that the Father's saving purpose had failed.
It was the very place where that purpose was being accomplished.
Peter later declared that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, while those who crucified Him remained responsible for their wicked actions (Acts 2:23).
Human evil was real.
The suffering was real.
The injustice was real.
But none of it overturned the saving plan of God.
And then came the resurrection.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
The crucified Christ was alive.
What appeared to be the greatest defeat became the proclamation of the greatest victory.
That is why Romans 8:31 cannot be separated from Romans 8:32.
Paul continues:
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” — Romans 8:32 (KJV)
There it is.
The foundation of Paul's confidence was not a trouble-free life.
It was the cross of Jesus Christ.
Paul was not asking believers to trust that their circumstances would always feel favorable.
He was asking them to look at what God had already done.
If the Father did not withhold His own Son when our salvation required such a costly sacrifice, we have profound reason to trust His commitment to complete His saving work.
But even here, we must be careful.
“All things” does not mean God has promised every luxury, every promotion, every relationship, or every earthly desire.
Romans 8 is concerned with God's saving purpose, the inheritance of His children, and the final glory awaiting those who are in Christ.
God has promised everything necessary to bring His people into the fullness of that redemption.
He has not promised to fulfill every expectation we bring to Him.
Sometimes the answer to prayer is deliverance from a trial.
Sometimes it is sustaining grace within the trial.
Paul knew the difference.
In 2 Corinthians 12, he describes pleading with the Lord three times for his thorn in the flesh to depart.
And the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
The thorn remained.
The grace remained too.
And grace proved sufficient.
Perhaps that is the part of faith we struggle to accept.
We want God to prove He is for us by removing everything that hurts.
But sometimes His faithfulness is revealed not by the immediate removal of the burden, but by His sustaining presence while we carry it.
That does not make the pain imaginary.
It does not make injustice acceptable.
It does not mean we should remain in abusive or dangerous situations rather than seeking protection.
And it certainly does not mean every tragedy is a punishment from God.
It means our suffering cannot be used as a simple measurement of whether Christ loves us.
Someone needs to hear that.
Especially the believer who has been quietly wondering whether God is angry because life has become so difficult.
Especially the mother who prays beside a hospital bed.
The father who feels ashamed because he cannot provide everything his family needs.
The young person fighting temptation while everyone around them seems to be celebrating it.
The Christian who is exhausted from trying to do what is right and being misunderstood anyway.
The person who still worships on Sunday but cries alone on Monday.
Your suffering does not automatically mean God has turned against you.
And your unanswered questions do not place you beyond His mercy.
But Paul goes even deeper.
Romans 8:33 asks:
“Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth.” (KJV)
Now the language changes.
The battlefield becomes a courtroom.
And this is where Paul's words become intensely personal.
Because some of our most painful enemies are not standing in front of us.
Some of them live in our memories.
A sin we cannot forget.
A failure we cannot undo.
A decision that destroyed someone's trust.
A secret we have hidden beneath years of religious activity.
A past we fear would change everyone's opinion of us if they knew the truth.
Sometimes the voice against us is another person's accusation.
Sometimes it is our own conscience, reminding us of what we have done.
And sometimes we confuse genuine conviction from God with the hopeless message that we can never be forgiven.
But Scripture makes an essential distinction.
Sin is serious.
Guilt is not something to excuse or decorate with spiritual language.
We really have sinned against a holy God.
Paul already established that in Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
No one escapes that verdict by being religious.
No one can manufacture righteousness through good behavior.
No one can purchase forgiveness through generosity, ministry involvement, or public displays of faith.
Our need is greater than self-improvement.
We need reconciliation with God.
And this is precisely why Jesus came.
The gospel does not announce that our sins were harmless.
It announces that Christ died for sinners.
His grace is not permission to remain comfortably in rebellion.
It is the undeserved mercy that calls us out of darkness and into a transformed life.
And when a sinner repents and trusts in Jesus Christ, their hope rests not in the strength of their performance but in the finished work of their Savior.
Paul asks:
“Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.” — Romans 8:34 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ reigns.
Christ intercedes.
The One who has every right to judge is the very One who gave Himself to save.
That does not mean wrongdoing has no consequences.
A forgiven person may still need to confess, make restitution where possible, accept accountability, and live with painful earthly consequences.
But for those who are truly in Christ, condemnation no longer has the final word.
Romans 8 began with this declaration:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
And by the time Paul reaches verse 34, he shows why that declaration stands.
Because Jesus Christ is not merely the subject of our religious inspiration.
He is our crucified and risen Savior.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not because the scandal was small.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because the mercy of God in Jesus Christ is greater than the guilt we could never erase ourselves.
Consider Peter.
He once spoke as though his loyalty could never fail.
He insisted he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
But before the rooster crowed, he denied knowing Jesus three times.
Imagine the sound of that rooster.
Imagine the realization.
Imagine the terrible memory of your own voice denying the One you claimed to love.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Those were not the tears of a man who had merely made a small mistake.
Those were the tears of someone who had seen the truth about himself.
And perhaps you know something about that kind of moment.
When the excuses finally stop working.
When the image you carefully built collapses.
When you realize that your problem is not simply what others have done to you, but what sin has done within you.
Peter could not undo his denial.
But his story did not end beside that fire.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Lord asked Peter three times whether he loved Him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had publicly denied Jesus was graciously restored to service.
His failure was not rewritten as faithfulness.
His sin was not called harmless.
He was restored by the Savior he had denied.
That is the beauty of grace.
It tells the truth about what happened without surrendering the future to what happened.
And if you are reading this with a past that still makes you ashamed, hear the invitation of the gospel.
You do not need to pretend you were innocent.
You need the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
You do not need to defend what God is calling you to confess.
You need to turn toward the mercy made available through Jesus Christ.
You do not need a carefully edited testimony.
You need redemption.
Because Jesus does not save us by pretending the scandal never happened.
He saves us by bearing sin, defeating death, and giving new life to those who trust in Him.
But what about the enemies who are still there?
The person who lied about you.
The family member who wounded you.
The friend who disappeared when you needed them most.
The people who rejoice when you stumble.
The opposition that seems to become louder every time you try to obey God.
Paul does not ignore them.
He asks another question.
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” — Romans 8:35 (KJV)
Look at that list.
Tribulation.
Distress.
Persecution.
Famine.
Nakedness.
Danger.
The sword.
These are not the words of a man who expects Christians to live without enemies.
These are the words of a man who understands that belonging to Jesus can bring a person into conflict with the world.
And then Paul quotes Psalm 44:22:
“For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” — Romans 8:36 (KJV)
Paul is not describing a life of uninterrupted earthly success.
He is describing faithful people who may suffer terribly.
Some may even be killed.
And then, astonishingly, he writes:
Not away from all these things.
Not after escaping every one of these things.
In all these things.
The Greek expression is:
“ὑπερνικῶμεν” — hypernikōmen.
It comes from a verb meaning to prevail decisively, to be more than victorious.
But notice the final words of the verse.
“Through him that loved us.”
Paul does not locate the believer's victory in human toughness, positive thinking, or the ability to overpower every opponent.
Our victory is through Christ.
The One who loved us.
The One who gave Himself for us.
The One whose resurrection guarantees that death will not have the last word over His people.
This is not a promise that every Christian will win every earthly battle.
Faithful believers can lose their jobs.
They can experience injustice.
They can suffer illness.
They can be imprisoned.
They can die.
The early church knew these realities.
And yet Paul declares that none of these things can finally separate those who belong to Christ from His saving love.
That is a victory much deeper than the world usually understands.
Because the world often defines victory as making your enemies watch you succeed.
Jesus teaches us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44).
The world says victory is revenge.
The gospel teaches forgiveness without denying the need for justice.
The world says victory means never appearing weak.
Paul learned that Christ's power is made perfect in weakness.
The world says victory is getting the last word.
The gospel says the risen Christ already has the final word.
And this should change the way we pray.
Instead of only praying, “Lord, destroy everyone who opposes me,” perhaps we also need to pray:

“Lord, protect me from evil. Give me wisdom to recognize danger. Help me stand firm in truth. Keep bitterness from taking root in my heart. Teach me to forgive without abandoning righteous boundaries. Correct me where I am wrong. And make me more like Jesus, even when others refuse to change.”
Because not everyone who disagrees with us is an enemy.
Not every closed door is a spiritual attack.
Not every criticism is persecution.
Sometimes correction is exactly what we need.
Sometimes the uncomfortable truth spoken by another person is one of the ways God exposes our pride.
Romans 8:31 is not permission to assume that God approves of every decision we make.
It is not a spiritual weapon for silencing accountability.
And it is not a guarantee that our personal ambitions will succeed simply because we attach God's name to them.
The promise belongs within the context of God's redeeming work in Christ.
That is why Romans 8:28 must also be read carefully.
“And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.” (KJV)
Paul does not say all things are good.
Betrayal is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Sin is evil.
But God is able to work through circumstances, including suffering, toward His ultimate good purpose for those who belong to Him.
And what is that purpose?
The next verse tells us.
Romans 8:29 speaks of believers being conformed to the image of God's Son.
The ultimate good is not merely that life becomes comfortable.
It is that God's people become like Jesus and are brought into the glory He has promised.
Sometimes that transformation is painfully slow.
Sometimes it happens through prayers we would never have chosen to pray.
Sometimes God exposes pride, resentment, self-reliance, hidden sin, and false sources of security.
Not every hardship can be traced to a specific lesson.
We should never presume to explain another person's suffering as though we know God's secret reasons.
But Scripture gives believers a sure hope: suffering cannot frustrate God's final purpose for those He has called in Christ.
And perhaps the most moving part of Romans 8 is that Paul knows how weak we can become along the way.
Earlier in the chapter, he writes:
There are moments when you do not have a powerful prayer.
You have tears.
You have exhaustion.
You have a heart so overwhelmed that even simple sentences feel impossible.
You sit on the edge of your bed.
The room is quiet.
Everyone thinks you are holding yourself together.
But you know how close you are to breaking.
And all you can manage is:
“Jesus, help me.”
Romans 8 does not shame that weakness.
It reminds believers that the Holy Spirit helps them in it.
You are not saved by how beautifully you pray.
You are not kept by how impressively you appear to handle suffering.
Your hope is in the God who saves through Jesus Christ and sustains His children by His Spirit.
And if your heart has become cold toward Him, the answer is not to hide behind religious language.
Come honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Seek wise counsel where counsel is needed.
Receive the truth of Scripture rather than the lies of despair.
There is no spiritual strength in pretending you are never wounded.
And there is no shame in needing the grace that every Christian depends upon.
Maybe that is why this verse matters so much.
Because sooner or later, everyone discovers that life contains enemies we cannot simply defeat through determination.
We cannot negotiate with death.
We cannot erase the past.
We cannot make every person love us.
We cannot guarantee tomorrow.
We cannot save ourselves from sin.
But the gospel announces a Savior who has accomplished what we could never accomplish.
Jesus Christ lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to all who repent and believe.
That is the heart of the Christian message, not the promise of a painless life.
And it is why Paul can finish Romans 8 with words that have comforted generations of suffering believers.
“For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 8:38–39 (KJV)
Think about what Paul includes.
Death.
Life.
The present.
The future.
Powers beyond our control.
Every created thing.
And then think about what he does not include.
He does not say believers will never encounter these things.
He says none of them can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is the promise.
Not that you will never be surrounded.
But that Christ will not abandon His own.
Not that nobody will ever accuse you.
But that no accusation can overturn God's justification of those who are in Christ.
Not that you will never be wounded.
But that your wounds cannot cancel the resurrection.
Not that you will never lose anything in this world.
But that nothing in creation can steal the eternal inheritance secured through Jesus Christ.
And suddenly Paul's question becomes even more powerful.
If God is for us, who can be against us?
People can be against us.
Circumstances can be against us.
Persecutors can be against us.
The devil can oppose us.
Death itself remains an enemy until its final defeat.
But none of them is greater than the crucified and risen Christ.
None can successfully overthrow God's saving purpose.
None can separate those who belong to Jesus from His love.
And none can erase what His grace has accomplished.
There is something else you need to know.
Being on God's side is not the same thing as assuming God is on the side of everything you want.
The question is not whether you can persuade God to endorse your plans.
The question is whether you have surrendered your life to Jesus Christ.
Have you repented of your sins?
Are you trusting Him as Savior and Lord?
Are you following His truth, even when it confronts you?
Because Romans 8 is not a blanket promise of divine approval for every person regardless of their relationship to Christ.
It is the assurance of God's saving love for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And if you do not yet belong to Him, the gospel is not telling you to manufacture confidence in yourself.
It is inviting you to come to the Savior.
You may have spent years fighting enemies outside of you while ignoring the sin within you.
You may have wanted God to defeat everyone who hurt you while resisting His call to forgive.
You may have wanted protection from consequences without surrendering the behavior that caused them.
You may have worn Christianity publicly while keeping Jesus at a distance privately.
But today, you can stop pretending.
You can bring your real life to Christ.
The anger.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The secret compromise.
The guilt.
The fear.
The broken trust.
The spiritual exhaustion.
Not to excuse these things.
Not to glorify them.
But to confess your need for the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
You do not have to clean yourself up to earn the right to come to Jesus.
You come to Him because you cannot save yourself.
And the grace that receives repentant sinners also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
That is redemption.
That is transformation.
That is the journey from scandal to grace.
And it begins and continues with Jesus Christ.
Maybe as you have been reading, someone has come to mind.
A friend who has stopped attending church because life became too painful.
A brother who thinks God has abandoned him.
A sister whose faith is barely holding together.
A parent quietly carrying burdens the family never sees.
Someone who believes that because they have enemies, they must have lost God's favor.
Do not assume they already know what Scripture says.
Sometimes discipleship begins with a conversation.
Sometimes encouragement begins with a message.
You do not need to reveal private details. You do not need to perform your pain for strangers. A few honest words are enough.
Someone else may need to hear that faithfulness is possible even when circumstances remain difficult.
Not because these words have any power apart from the truth they communicate, but because there may come a night when you need to open Romans 8 again and remember what God has actually promised.
When the accusation returns.
When the fear becomes loud.
When someone walks away.
When the prayer seems unanswered.
Come back to the Word.
Read the whole chapter.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of the gospel.
We want those resources to remain accessible to people who need biblical encouragement and teaching.
And that is where I want to speak to you personally for a moment.
Every article shared, every resource prepared, every person reached, and every effort to continue and expand this ministry requires time, work, and practical support.
Scripture gives us a meaningful foundation for supporting those who labor in teaching the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
But we also need to honor what Scripture says about giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not make you more loved by Jesus.
And it is not a substitute for every other responsibility of biblical generosity, including supporting your local church and caring for those in need.
These items are simply products and resources, not objects that confer spiritual blessing. The real treasure remains the gospel of Jesus Christ.
Financial support matters, but so do the people who quietly encourage others toward Christ without ever receiving recognition.
We never want anyone to feel that access to the love of God depends on their ability to give money.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Salvation is not for sale.
Grace is not for sale.
And the gospel must always remain greater than the platform through which it is shared.
And now, before you go, I want you to remember the person who first opened this article.
The person who wondered why life was so difficult if God was truly for them.
Maybe that person is still you.
Maybe your circumstances have not changed in the minutes it took you to read these words.
The problem is still waiting.
The enemy has not apologized.
The grief has not disappeared.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The door has not opened.
And the future is still uncertain.
I will not tell you that tomorrow everything will suddenly make sense.
Paul did not promise that.
Jesus did not promise that.
But there is something infinitely more certain than tomorrow's circumstances.
The Son of God was crucified.
He rose from the dead.
He reigns at the right hand of the Father.
And He intercedes for those who belong to Him.
If you are in Christ, your present suffering is not the final chapter of your story.
If you have wandered from Him, do not turn this promise into an excuse to remain far away. Hear His call to repentance and faith.
If you have fallen, do not defend your sin. Bring it into the light and seek His mercy.
If you have been wounded, do not confuse another person's cruelty with the character of your Savior.
And if you are standing in the middle of a battle you never wanted, remember this:
The promise was never that nobody would come against you.
The promise is that no enemy can ultimately defeat the saving purpose of the God who has given His Son for you.
That is why we can say with Paul:
“If God be for us, who can be against us?”
Not because we are invincible.
But because Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death.
Not because we deserve His faithfulness.
But because His mercy is greater than our merit.
Not because our story contains no scandal.
But because grace has entered the story through the cross.
And the One who died and rose again is able to bring His people all the way home.
The enemies you face may still be standing when the night is over—but the tomb they could never keep closed has been empty for nearly two thousand years.
